extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers and natural philosophers seeking to be convinced of a Creator (skeptics/atheists; readers of 18th-century natural-philosophy/apologetic works)
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th‑century apologetic treatise that uses contemporary natural philosophy (astronomy, optics, hydrostatics, particle theory) to argue for the existence and attributes of a Creator and to answer atheistical objections. It develops methodological and evidential principles for evaluating astronomical and physical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of hypothesis is not proof of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplicity of an hypothesis is not always an argument of its truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a hypothesis merely because it is more simple or 'becoming the wisdom of the Creator'; simplicity may aid conception but does not demonstrate reality. Examples: circular vs elliptical orbits — the circle is simpler but not therefore true. (See Sec. XI.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses may be adopted for convenience, not as assertions of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians frequently employ hypotheses known to be false or only provisional for the convenience of calculations; using an hypothesis in computations does not mean one asserts its literal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the distinction between practical/adaptive hypotheses used to make calculations tractable and claims of ontological truth. The text cites Copernicus, Tycho, Cassini, and others who use differing hypotheses depending on convenience (e.g., fictitious circles, assumed parallels in dialling, simplified projectile trajectories). Do not conflate methodological convenience with established fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational certainty depends on instruments and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The reliability and precision of observational claims must be judged by the quality of instruments and methods used; more exact instruments yield more certain results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measurements made with superior methods (telescopes armed with micrometers, pendulum clocks, methods using lunar distances) over ancient large-instrument observations. The text emphasizes that improvements (telescopes, micrometers) have steadily reduced parallax estimates and increased certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric/trigonometric method for computing solar semidiameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the measured horizontal parallax and the apparent semidiameter of the Sun, together with the Earth's semidiameter, in triangle relations to compute the Sun's real semidiameter and distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: (I) take Earth's semidiameter as unit; (II) measure horizontal parallax (angle ACB) and apparent semidiameter (angle DBC); (III) by trigonometry (two angles and one side) determine BC (distance) and then DC (real semidiameter). The author notes using angle proportions (rule of three) instead of sines is acceptable with negligible difference for practical computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small errors in parallax produce very large errors in computed volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because body volumes scale as the cubes of semidiameters, tiny differences in measured parallaxes (seconds of arc) lead to enormous multiplicative differences in inferred planetary magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when interpreting claimed sizes: the text demonstrates examples where different parallax values produce Sun-volume estimates ranging from tens of thousands to millions of Earth‑volumes (e.g., factors like ~31,000; ~900,000; ~4,000,000). Thus evaluate sensitivity to parallax error before accepting quantitative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eclipse geometry as evidence that the Sun is larger than the Earth
rubrics_metrics.description: The tapering shape of Earth's shadow during lunar eclipses (a pyramidal/conical shadow ALZ) demonstrates that the Sun's diameter must be larger than the Earth's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the observed behavior of lunar-eclipse shadows (they decrease toward the vertex rather than increase) to infer relative sizes: if the Sun were as small or smaller than Earth, the shadow behavior would differ. This is given as an accessible and convincing geometrical demonstration (Sec. III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare generations' methods to interpret apparent disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between ancient and modern astronomical results often reflect inferior instruments/methods of the ancients rather than true scientific disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering divergent historical values (e.g., for parallax or apparent diameter), examine methods: the ancients' large instruments could not measure to a minute or second, while modern telescopes and micrometers permit far finer determinations. The text argues the modern trend toward smaller parallax values is due to better technique, not mere contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical adequacy of a hypothesis does not establish its ontological truth
rubrics_metrics.description: If an hypothesis enables calculations that agree with observations, that practical success is not sufficient to claim the hypothesis is true in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly warns that astronomers may prefer hypotheses that simplify computation (and thereby fit data) while acknowledging those hypotheses may be fictitious; thus one must not accept a cosmological claim as proved solely because it yields correct predictive calculations (see discussion of Copernicus' preface and practice among mathematicians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand solid experimental proof before asserting universal motions (e.g., Earth's motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about fundamental motions (such as whether the Earth moves) require decisive experimental demonstration; in the absence of such proof, prudence demands withholding categorical assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that leading astronomers differ and some admit uncertainty; fixed-star parallax remains effectively unobserved with decisive certainty, so the question is still open experimentally. The burden of proof lies with those claiming demonstrable motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughly answer objections by specific rebuttal and demonstration in apologetic argument
rubrics_metrics.description: To convince skeptics, one should reply to common objections point-by-point using experiments, observations, reasoned demonstrations, and where relevant physical hypotheses (e.g., particle theory to answer objections about resurrection and persistence of identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise models addressing multiple named objections (e.g., about smallness and attrition of particles with respect to resurrection) and supplies experimental, geometrical, and metaphysical responses. The guidance is to structure apologetic argument as a series of specific answers rather than broad assertions.
